positions.text: Vu, Zhang, and Aberer independently instantiate a narrower version of Kaal's two-ended temporal constraint. Their provider-selection protocol considers only the provider's most recent interaction and can blacklist a provider after recent cheating, so a large stock of older standing cannot indefinitely mask current behavior. Separately, a provider's pseudonym acquires an identity premium that increases with tenure; leaving and rejoining forfeits that accumulated value, making whitewashing non-optimal for a rational provider. This qualifies rather than fully validates Kaal's design: the source models a human service marketplace, uses a most-recent-rating rule rather than continuous score decay, and imposes an economic identity premium rather than Kaal's non-transferable REP and broader institutional history.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Specifically, the reliability of the most recent rating on each eligible provider is evaluated to determine whether the provider defected in the last transaction with a previous client.
Interestingly, the consideration of only the most recent rating gives sufficient incentives for rational providers to cooperate in most of their transactions.
Essentially, Definition 3 specifies that for the selection of a provider, only the last interaction (from any client) with that provider is taken into consideration

Under this pricing scheme, an initially cheap pseudonym would have an increasingly significant value over time, thereby effectively eliminating the incentive of switching identities and whitewashing bad behavior of any opportunistic provider.

even if establishing new identities is relatively cheap, it is expected that every rational provider finds it optimal to keep the same identity for the whole lifetime rather than cheating, leaving and joining with a new identity.
